title: IP Addressing & Subnetting
subtitle: Classes, CIDR masks, network/broadcast math, private ranges & IPv6 - the computational core of the AXIS networking bucket

readingSections.title: What Is an IP Address?
readingSections.quickSummary: A 32-bit number in four dotted octets (0-255 each) that uniquely identifies a device on an IP network.
content: An IP address is the logical address that identifies a device on a network so packets know where to travel. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long, written as four decimal octets separated by dots - for example 192.168.1.77. Each octet is 8 bits and ranges from 0 to 255, giving 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 possible addresses.

Every address has two parts: the NETWORK portion (which street) and the HOST portion (which house). The subnet mask draws the line between them - mask bits are 1 for the network part and 0 for the host part.
Machines read addresses in BINARY; humans read dotted decimal. The exam asks you to translate between the two, so the place-value row 128-64-32-16-8-4-2-1 must be automatic.

subsections.title: Logical vs physical
subsections.content: IP addresses are LOGICAL - assigned by software (DHCP or an admin) and changeable. MAC addresses are PHYSICAL - burned into the NIC and (normally) permanent. ARP maps IP -> MAC on the local network; that pairing question is a classic MCQ.

quickRevision: IPv4 = 32 bits = 4 octets x 8 bits, each 0-255.
Network portion + host portion; the subnet mask marks the boundary.
tricks: To read any mask octet, add the place values of its 1-bits from the left: 11110000 -> 128+64+32+16 = 240.
255 = all eight 1s; 0 = all zeros; anything else means a subnetted octet.
If a question says 'permanent, burned-in address' -> MAC. 'Can be assigned by DHCP' -> IP.
patterns: 'How many bits in an IPv4 address?' - 32.

pyqPatterns.question: An IP address is a ___ bit address.

readingSections.companyNote: One or two definition-level IP questions appear in the AXIS networking bucket - free marks from this section alone.

readingSections.title: The Five Address Classes
readingSections.quickSummary: First octet decides the class: A 1-126 (/8), B 128-191 (/16), C 192-223 (/24), D 224-239 (multicast), E 240-255 (experimental).
content: Classful addressing splits the IPv4 space by the FIRST octet. Class A: 1-126, default mask 255.0.0.0 (/8) - 16 million hosts per network, for giants. Class B: 128-191, mask 255.255.0.0 (/16) - 65,534 hosts. Class C: 192-223, mask 255.255.255.0 (/24) - 254 hosts, for small networks.

Class D (224-239) is reserved for MULTICAST groups - never assigned to hosts. Class E (240-255) is experimental/research - also never for hosts. The missing 127 block is the LOOPBACK network (127.0.0.1 = 'this machine'), and 0.x.x.x is reserved.
Memory hooks: 1-126 A (127 missing for loopback), 128-191 B, 192-223 C, 224+ D/E. 'A few large, B medium, C many small.'

subsections.title: The class table
subsections.content:
Class A: first octet 1-126, /8, 255.0.0.0, ~16.7M hosts/network
Class B: 128-191, /16, 255.255.0.0, 65,534 hosts
Class C: 192-223, /24, 255.255.255.0, 254 hosts
Class D: 224-239 - multicast, no mask
Class E: 240-255 - experimental/reserved

subsections.title: Why 127 is missing from A
subsections.content: 127.0.0.0/8 is the loopback block - traffic sent there never leaves the machine. 127.0.0.1 is 'localhost'. That is why Class A ends at 126, and why 'which address tests your own NIC?' answers 127.0.0.1.

quickRevision: Hosts per network: A ~16.7M, B 65,534, C 254.
tricks: First-octet boundaries rhyme with powers: 126/127 cut, 128 start of B, 191 end of B (191 = 256-64-1), 192 start of C, 223 end of C.
224 = multicast (Class D) - the number 224 itself is the giveaway in stems.
'Which class does 140.x.x.x belong to?' - 140 sits in 128-191 -> B. Just place the first octet on the number line.
patterns: 'Which address tests the local TCP/IP stack?' - 127.0.0.1.

pyqPatterns.question: Identify the class of a given IP (e.g., 140.10.2.1).
pyqPatterns.approach: Read the first octet against the number line: 140 -> Class B.

readingSections.companyNote: Class identification from the first octet is the single most repeated IP MCQ across placement papers.

readingSections.title: Subnetting: Masks, CIDR & Network Math
readingSections.quickSummary: /n sets n mask bits; mask octet = 256 - block size; network = floor(ip/block) x block; hosts = 2^h - 2.
content: Subnetting borrows bits from the host portion to create smaller networks. CIDR notation /n says how many 1-bits the mask has: /24 = 24 ones = 255.255.255.0. Every borrowed bit DOUBLES the number of subnets and HALVES each subnet's size.

Three mechanical steps answer any subnet question. (1) Mask: fill n ones from the left; any partially-filled octet equals 256 minus the block size. (2) Network address: block = 2^(32-n) in the last significant octet; network = floor(my-ip / block) x block. (3) Broadcast = next network minus 1; usable hosts = network+1 through broadcast-1.
Host count formula: usable hosts = 2^h - 2 where h = 32 - n host bits - subtracting the network address (all host bits 0) and broadcast (all host bits 1).

subsections.title: Worked example: 172.16.50.172/20
subsections.content:
/20 -> mask 255.255.240.0 (third octet 11110000 = 240).
Block in third octet = 256 - 240 = 16 -> boundaries .0, .16, .32, .48, .64 ...
50 falls between 48 and 64 -> network = 172.16.48.0.
Broadcast = 172.16.63.255. Usable range = 172.16.48.1 - 172.16.63.254.
Wildcard (for ACLs) = 0.0.15.255 - the inverse of the mask.

subsections.title: The published PYQ walkthrough
subsections.content: 'Deny the /20 subnet containing 172.16.50.172' -> network 172.16.48.0, wildcard 0.0.15.255 -> access-list 10 deny 172.16.48.0 0.0.15.255. The distractor 172.16.64.0 starts one block too high - floor(50/16) = 48, never 64.

quickRevision: /n = n mask ones. Partial octet value = 256 - block.
Block = 2^(32-n). Network = floor(ip/block) x block. Broadcast = next network - 1.
tricks: Mask-octet pairs come in sum-256 pairs: 240<->16, 192<->64, 252<->4, 248<->8. Know one, know both.
For 'which subnet contains X', divide the relevant octet by the block and keep the floor - never round up.
Hosts formula: subtract 2 ALWAYS (network + broadcast). Options offering 2^h without -2 are the trap.
/30 = 2 usable hosts - the router-to-router link size; it appears as a 'smallest subnet' answer.
patterns: 'Which subnet does X belong to?' - floor division by the block.
'Wildcard mask for the ACL' - inverse of the subnet mask.
'Broadcast address of X/n' - next network minus one.

pyqPatterns.source: Asked in Accenture AXIS Technical Assessment (Cisco-style)
pyqPatterns.question: Standard access list denying the /20 subnet of 172.16.50.172?
Wildcard/mask conversion for a given CIDR.
pyqPatterns.approach: Mask octet + wildcard octet = 255 in every fully-used octet position; block pairs sum to 256.

readingSections.companyNote: Subnet membership + wildcard conversion is THE computational question of the AXIS networking bucket - practise the floor-division method until it takes under 30 seconds.

readingSections.title: Private & Special Addresses
readingSections.quickSummary: RFC 1918 private blocks: 10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 - not routable on the Internet. Plus loopback, APIPA and broadcast/network rules.
content: Three blocks are reserved for PRIVATE networks (RFC 1918) and are never routed on the public Internet: 10.0.0.0/8 (10.0.0.0-10.255.255.255), 172.16.0.0/12 (172.16.0.0-172.31.255.255 - only the 172.16-31 second octet, NOT all of 172.x), and 192.168.0.0/16. Home routers and offices hand these out; NAT translates them to public IPs.

Special addresses: 127.0.0.1 loopback (test your own stack); 169.254.x.x APIPA - the self-assigned address a Windows machine gives itself when DHCP fails (a favourite MCQ); x.x.x.255 subnet broadcast (delivered to every host in the subnet); x.x.x.0 the network address itself (never assigned to a host).
Everything else in the IPv4 space is PUBLIC - globally unique, Internet-routable, leased from an ISP/registry. 8.8.8.8 (Google DNS) is public; 192.168.1.1 (typical home router) is private.

subsections.title: The 172 trap
subsections.content:
PRIVATE: 172.16.0.0 through 172.31.255.255 only.
PUBLIC: 172.0.x.x-172.15.x.x and 172.32.x.x-172.255.x.x.
MCQs offer 172.32.5.4 as a 'private' distractor - it is PUBLIC (32 > 31).

subsections.title: APIPA - the DHCP failure address
subsections.content: When a DHCP server cannot be reached, Windows self-assigns 169.254.x.x/16 (Automatic Private IP Addressing). Seeing 169.254 on a machine = DHCP problem. Classic exam question with a one-line answer.

quickRevision: Host bits all-0 = network address; all-1 = broadcast - neither is assignable to a host.
NAT translates private -> public for Internet access.
tricks: The 172 rule: private only when the SECOND octet is 16-31. Write '172.16-31' on your scratch pad.
169.254 in the stem -> DHCP failure/APIPA - answer without reading the options.
All-ones host portion -> broadcast; all-zeros -> network. Both unassignable.
patterns: 'Which is a private address?' - check the three blocks; 172.32+ and 172.0-15 are public traps.
'Machine self-assigned 169.254.20.1 - what does it mean?' - DHCP server unreachable.
'Which address is not routable on the Internet?' - any RFC 1918 private block.

readingSections.title: IPv6 Essentials
readingSections.quickSummary: 128 bits, eight hex groups colon-separated; '::' compresses ONE run of zero groups; loopback ::1; no broadcast (multicast instead).
content: IPv6 addresses the IPv4 exhaustion problem with 128 bits - about 340 undecillion addresses. Written as EIGHT groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons: 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329.

Two compression rules: leading zeros in a group may be dropped (0db8 -> db8, 0042 -> 42), and ONE continuous run of all-zero groups may be replaced by a double colon - so the example becomes 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329. The double colon may appear only ONCE (ambiguity rule).

Address types: unicast (one), multicast (many), and anycast (nearest of many). There is NO broadcast in IPv6 - its job is done by multicast (the all-nodes group ff02::1). Loopback is ::1 (not 127.0.0.1), and the unspecified address is ::.

subsections.title: Compression worked example
subsections.content:
Full: 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329
Drop leading zeros: 2001:db8:0:0:0:ff00:42:8329
Compress the zero run once: 2001:db8::ff00:42:8329
Illegal: 2001::db8::ff00:42:8329 (double colon twice).

subsections.title: Key addresses
subsections.content:
Loopback: ::1 (equivalent of IPv4's 127.0.0.1).
Unspecified: :: (means 'no address' - never assigned).
All-nodes multicast: ff02::1.
Link-local: fe80::/10 - self-configured per interface.
Global unicast: currently 2000::/3.

quickRevision: Drop leading zeros; '::' replaces ONE zero run, used at most once.
Loopback ::1; no broadcast - multicast ff02::1 instead.
tricks: Double-colon questions: the answer is always 'once only' - two double colons is ambiguous and illegal.
'IPv6 has no broadcast' - it uses multicast instead; that sentence is a ready-made MCQ.
patterns: 'Compress this address' - drop leading zeros, then :: the single zero run.

pyqPatterns.question: IPv6 address length and notation questions.
pyqPatterns.approach: 128 bits, hex/colon, single :: compression, ::1 loopback, no broadcast.

readingSections.companyNote: One light IPv6 question (bits, :: rule or loopback) shows up in most networking buckets - three facts cover it.

formulas.title: Octet Binary Place Values

formula.text: Each octet is 8 bits with place values 128 down to 1; sum the 1-bit positions to read the decimal.

formulas.whenToUse: Converting between dotted decimal and binary, and reading mask octets.
explanation: Write the eight place values, put the bits under them, add where 1.
formulas.commonMistake: Reversing bit order - the 128 place is always leftmost.

formulas.title: Class Identification Table

formula.text: Read the FIRST octet: 1-126 A, 128-191 B, 192-223 C, 224-239 D (multicast), 240-255 E.

formulas.whenToUse: Any 'which class is this IP' question.
explanation: 127 is loopback, so A stops at 126.
D = multicast groups; E = experimental - neither for hosts.
Hosts per network: A 16,777,214; B 65,534; C 254.
formulas.commonMistake: Calling 127.x Class A loopback 'A range' - it is reserved out of A.

formulas.title: CIDR to Mask & Wildcard

formula.text: /n fills n ones; each mask octet is the sum of its place values; wildcard is the octet-wise inverse.

formulas.whenToUse: Converting /n to dotted mask, or producing ACL wildcards.
formulas.commonMistake: Writing the wildcard as the mask - they are inverses.

formulas.title: Usable Hosts & Block Size

formula.text: Usable hosts subtract the network and broadcast addresses from the block.

explanation: Block size in the significant octet = 256 - mask octet: 240 -> 16, 192 -> 64.
Every borrowed bit doubles subnets and halves block size.
formulas.memoryTip: Minus 2, always - network and broadcast live there.
formulas.commonMistake: Answering 64 for /26 hosts - that is the block size, not usable hosts.

formulas.title: Network & Broadcast by Floor Division

formula.text: Divide the key octet by the block, keep the floor, multiply back; broadcast is the next network minus one.

formulas.whenToUse: 'Which subnet contains X?' and broadcast-address questions.

formulas.title: RFC 1918 & Special Address Table
explanation: 127.0.0.1 loopback; 169.254.x.x APIPA (DHCP failed); host-bits-all-1 = broadcast; all-0 = network.
formulas.memoryTip: 172.16-31: write the range, test the second octet.
formulas.commonMistake: Treating all of 172.x as private - only 16-31 is.

exp: /30 = exactly 2 usable hosts - one per router, zero waste.

mcqs.q: The IPv6 all-nodes multicast address (broadcast replacement) is:
exp: ff02::1 reaches all nodes on the link - IPv6's broadcast substitute.
::1 is loopback; fe80::1 is a link-local unicast.

mcqs.q: A company leases 172.16.0.0/16 and must carve 100 subnets with the most hosts each. Borrowing 7 bits gives 128 subnets of:
exp: /16 + 7 = /23 -> 9 host bits -> 2^9 - 2 = 510 usable hosts per subnet.

mcqs.q: Which pair of addresses are BOTH public (Internet-routable)?
exp: 172.32 is outside 16-31 -> public; 192.169 is outside 192.168 -> public.
Every other option contains an RFC 1918 address.
